items.title: Miley Cyrus Announces New Album ‘Bass Persuades,’ Sets Two Shows for Hollywood Bowl
items.summary:
Miley Cyrus has announced a new album, "Bass Persuades," arriving September 18 on Atlantic Records, and two Hollywood Bowl concerts to go with it. The Spotify listing puts the record at 10 tracks, with guest appearances from Model/Actriz and Miike Snow's Andrew Wyatt.

Cyrus laid out what the title means to her in an Instagram post announcing the record. "Music takes hold of us. We feel it, sing it, sometimes dance to it, let it out and carry on. It is powerful, vulnerable, sweet and strong," she wrote, adding, "Heart full, heartache, every part of life in between. That's what the title means to me."

The Bowl dates, October 16 and 18, mark a rare live appearance, and her announcement suggests she will perform the album in full. Model/Actriz will join her as a special guest. "The Hollywood Bowl is my favorite place to experience music and see my favorite artists," Cyrus wrote. "I've sat in those seats many times, but I've never taken the stage. LA is my heart and I'm bringing it home."

Ticketing runs in stages: an Amex presale opens September 8 at 10 a.m. PT, Cyrus's own presale follows September 9 at the same hour, and Spotify will set aside a Reserved allotment for top fans. General onsale begins September 10 at 10 a.m. PT.

The rollout began Sunday, when Cyrus bought a wrap-around cover of the Los Angeles Times carrying only her face and her first name, and updated her website with the same image. She appears to have dropped her surname for this cycle, and a press release refers to her simply as Miley.

Variety recently confirmed that Cyrus signed with Atlantic after two albums on Columbia, including "Endless Summer Vacation" and its Grammy-winning single "Flowers." In a recent conversation with Daryl Hannah for Wonderland, she described songwriting as something closer to recall than invention: "A new song can feel like I've already heard it before."

items.title: Jonathan Bailey Drops Out Of West End Revival Of ‘Sunday In The Park With George’
items.summary:
Jonathan Bailey has withdrawn from the West End revival of "Sunday in the Park with George," following Ariana Grande's departure from the same production last month. Bailey announced the decision in a statement posted to his social accounts.

"Ari is one of my dearest friends, and my support for her is unwavering. Marianne is extraordinary and one of my longest collaborators and friends," Bailey wrote. "After much consideration, I have decided to also step back from Sunday in the Park with George."

Deadline, which reported the exit, first revealed in December that Grande and Bailey were considering reuniting on the Sondheim musical. Empire Street Productions and London's Barbican Centre confirmed the following month that they would stage it with the pair, targeting a summer 2027 opening.

Producers had held off on putting tickets on sale until after Grande's tour wrapped September 1 at London's O2 Arena. With both leads now gone, the production's plans are unresolved.

Bailey framed his departure as a handoff rather than an ending. "This brilliant, introspective musical has been a real passion project for me, and I feel incredibly lucky to have shared in its journey with this team," he wrote, saying he looked forward to what the team and the two actors who take on George and Dot will make of it.

items.title: Yeah Yeah Yeahs Release New Live Album and Concert Film
items.summary:
Yeah Yeah Yeahs have released "Hidden in Pieces (Live at the Royal Albert Hall)," a 13-track live album out now through Secretly Canadian, alongside a companion concert film. The recording documents the band's 2025 performance at the London venue, their first ever there, during the Hidden in Pieces tour.

That theatre run leaned on rare deep cuts and rearranged staples, backed by acoustic guitars, strings and piano. The setlist captured on the record moves from "In Heaven" and "Gold Lion" through a cover of Björk's "Hyperballad" and on to "Maps" and "Zero."

Karen O tied the project to a specific moment. "Hidden in Pieces Live at the Royal Albert Hall was born out of a need to commune with our band and fan family in 2025, after the election," she said in a statement, adding that "the real alchemy happened when we played the hall, it clicked into place. All the shows we performed on this small tour were extraordinarily vulnerable."

A physical edition and an expanded digital deluxe version arrive October 23, per Consequence. The deluxe adds nine tracks drawn from San Diego, the Beacon Theatre, the Chicago Theatre, Teatro Metropolitan and the Orpheum, plus two Sonic Ranch recordings.

The 22-minute film, "Hidden in Pieces," was shot at the Orpheum Theatre in Los Angeles at the close of the band's 25th anniversary tour and directed by Barnaby Clay. It is streaming on the Criterion Channel and will screen in select theatres in the US, UK, Australia, Mexico and Japan, several of them paired with a second feature chosen by the band — "Eraserhead" in Los Angeles, "Mulholland Drive" in Melbourne and Sydney, "Wings of Desire" in New York. Screening tickets go on sale September 3.

items.title: Duane “Keffe D” Davis Found Guilty of Orchestrating Tupac’s Murder
items.summary:
A Las Vegas jury found Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, guilty of first-degree murder on Monday in the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur. The verdict came a couple of hours after closing arguments in a two-week trial. Sentencing will take place at a later date, and Davis faces the possibility of life in prison.

Prosecutors Marc DiGiacomo and Binu Palal of the Clark County district attorney's office cast Davis as the shot caller who assembled the group and supplied the weapon. "(Davis) acquired firearms, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr. Shakur," Palal told jurors, according to reporting by Billboard cited by Consequence.

Defense attorney Michael Sanft argued that his client's account of the night, laid out in a 2019 memoir, was invention meant to draw money and attention, and told jurors a ghost-writer made up the incriminating passages. Sanft said Davis liked to "bullshit" and argued that "the state cannot prove to you beyond a reasonable doubt the claim that Keffe had anything to do with a first-degree murder."

Shakur was shot on September 7, 1996, hours after he and Death Row Records founder Marion "Suge" Knight beat Davis's nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, in the MGM Grand lobby following a Mike Tyson fight. The dispute traced back to an earlier attempt by Anderson to take a Death Row medallion from a Knight associate. Prosecutors said Davis gathered at least three others, tracked the pair down and handed a gun to someone in the back seat of the car that pulled alongside Knight's SUV. Shakur died six days later at 25.

Clark County prosecutors had suspected Davis for years but lacked the evidence to charge him until the memoir and a string of media appearances in which he discussed the shooting. A grand jury indicted him in 2023 on a charge of murder with a deadly weapon; Nevada law allows a person accused of arranging a killing to be charged as the killer. Davis has never publicly named the person who fired the shots.

Davis was sentenced in 2025 in an unrelated case involving a jail fight, receiving 16 to 40 months, and was granted parole earlier this year according to prison records.

items.title: California Lawmakers Pass Film Credit Fix on Tax Cap
items.summary:
The California Legislature has passed SB 186, a budget measure that lets studios convert their film and television tax credits to cash in two years rather than five. Both the Assembly and the state Senate cleared the bill before the end-of-session deadline at midnight Monday.

The fix responds to a $5 million annual cap on corporate tax credits that lawmakers imposed in June. The Motion Picture Association and the Entertainment Union Coalition warned that the cap would blunt the state's $750 million production incentive, and legislative leaders negotiated with the governor's office in response.

The compromise stops short of what the industry wanted. Independent film credits are fully exempt from the cap, and the expiration window for older non-refundable credits extends from nine years to as much as 15, but there is no blanket carveout for studios — state leaders declined, in part because the tech industry would have sought the same treatment.

MPA chief executive Charles Rivkin said Tuesday the agreement will maintain the program's competitiveness so creators keep making movies and shows in California. The Entertainment Union Coalition said its members sent roughly 450,000 letters to lawmakers, thanked authors Assemblyman Rick Chavez Zbur and Sen. Ben Allen along with Gov. Gavin Newsom, and signaled it will keep pressing on the incentive.

Separately, Variety reported that the Legislature approved AB 2319 on Sunday, a tax incentive aimed at post-production work backed by the Motion Picture Editors Guild and a coalition of post houses and VFX studios. The Senate passed it 33-5 and the Assembly concurred with the Senate's amendments 72-2.

Newsom has not taken a position on AB 2319 and has until September 30 to sign it. Its author, Assemblyman Nick Schultz, said Monday that if it becomes law the Legislature has agreed to put $10 million toward the program, well below the $100 million supporters sought.
